standard.title: Impacts of colonial development
standard.description: the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, the colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K03 (Experiences of colonisation) and AC9HS4K04 (Effects of contact and invasion): Students explain the experiences of colonisation for First Nations Australians and early colonists, and the effects of contact and invasion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment, identifying both intended and unintended consequences.

nodes.label: Impact on First Nations Australians
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial development on the lives of First Nations Australians, including dispossession, conflict, disruption to cultural practices and loss of life.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two impacts of colonial development on First Nations Australians.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of impacts on First Nations Australians: dispossession from Country, frontier conflict, disruption to cultural and spiritual practices, loss of life, and the destruction of established economic systems (including food sources and land management).
wider: Investigate the experience of a particular First Nations community or nation during colonial expansion, using primary and secondary sources to describe changes to their way of life
Examine First Nations Australian perspectives and responses to colonisation, including resistance movements and efforts to maintain cultural practices
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand colonial impacts only from a settler perspective will struggle to engage with the multi-perspective analysis required in subsequent nodes and in later HASS learning. A thin account here distorts the historical record and limits the sophistication of future causal analysis.

response_modes.reason: Multiple First Nations perspectives and case studies are essential — not as enrichment but as the corrective to a default settler-centred account. Use sources that foreground First Nations voices and experiences.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations specifically support investigation of particular First Nations communities and their responses to colonisation — this is a rich and important pedagogical direction that goes well beyond minimum and has significant cultural significance.
success_criteria: Students explain at least two specific impacts on First Nations Australians with reference to historical evidence.
Students describe how colonial development changed the relationship between First Nations Australians and their Country/Place.

nodes.label: Impact on colonists and convicts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the impact of colonial development on the daily lives of different groups of colonists and convicts, including differences in their clothing, food, work, housing and social position.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the daily life of one colonial group (e.g. convicts or free settlers) including at least three aspects of daily life.
nodes.typical_width: Compare the daily lives of different groups — convicts, free settlers, squatters, indentured labourers, and different migrant groups — across several aspects: clothing, food and water access, work (paid and unpaid), housing, leisure, and children's lives.
wider: Investigate the experiences of a specific migrant group (e.g. Chinese miners, Afghan cameleers, Pacific Islander labourers) and compare their colonial experience with that of British free settlers
Examine the role of women in colonial society, including both the constraints they faced and the agency they exercised across different social positions

response_modes.reason: The range of colonial groups is the key width dimension here — students benefit from comparing across multiple social positions rather than studying one group in depth. The elaborations explicitly name this range.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations name a rich range of colonial social groups and the comparison across them is a key historical thinking skill. Migrant group investigations and women's histories are particularly significant directions that add genuine breadth.
success_criteria: Students describe the daily life of at least two different colonial groups and identify at least one key difference between them.
Students use relevant historical terms (e.g. 'convict', 'free settler', 'squatter') accurately in their account.

nodes.label: Impact on the natural environment
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial settlement on the natural environment, including changes to vegetation, land use, fauna and ecosystems.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least one way colonial settlement changed the natural environment.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how colonial settlement patterns were shaped by geographical factors (land for farming, water, transport) and how these patterns impacted local environments through vegetation clearance, introduction of grazing livestock, drainage, and the effects on local flora, fauna and ecosystems.
wider: Compare the present and past landscape of a local area to identify changes in vegetation and fauna since European colonisation, using maps, photographs or local data
Examine the contrasting approaches to land management of First Nations Australians (e.g. firestick farming) and British colonists, and evaluate the long-term environmental consequences of each

response_modes.reason: Environmental impact is strongest when explored through local or regional examples — connecting abstract land-use changes to a specific place makes the impact tangible and supports geographical thinking.

success_criteria: Students describe at least two ways colonial settlement changed the natural environment.
Students explain how settlement patterns were influenced by geographical features.

nodes.label: Integrating multiple perspectives on impact
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial development in Australia on First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and the natural environment, presenting a multi-perspective account that acknowledges intended and unintended consequences.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the impact on at least two different groups and on the environment, and identify at least one unintended consequence.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the contrasting impacts on First Nations Australians, different colonial groups, and the environment; identify which impacts were intended by colonial authorities and which were unintended; acknowledge different perspectives on these impacts.
wider: Evaluate which group experienced the most significant negative impact from colonial development and justify the claim with evidence
Investigate how the long-term environmental impacts of colonial settlement continue to affect Australia today, and how First Nations land management practices are now being recognised and applied

response_modes.reason: This integration node requires students to hold multiple perspectives simultaneously — use structured comparison tasks (e.g. perspective matrices) that make visible the different experiences and their causes.

success_criteria: Students explain the impact on at least three groups or entities (e.g. First Nations Australians, convicts, environment) in an integrated account.
Students distinguish between intended and unintended consequences of colonial development.
Students demonstrate awareness that different groups experienced colonial development very differently.
